2026-11-15 design (services engineer; display.md v1.14): three options for the title in the compositor's own lines. (A) name it as ui.md §3.9 names a described value: `"`, C0/DEL/C1, U+2028/2029 and the bidi controls written [U+XXXX], plus every byte that does not begin a valid UTF-8 character as [U+FFFD] (the title is bytes, and a lone lead byte makes the narrator, user/apps/narrator/src/main.rs:55-65, swallow the closing quote); plain titles read as before; reversible by a version. (B) refuse CREATE_WINDOW/TITLE with such bytes: changes what every client may do under the frozen verbs (display.md v1.1/v1.3), and a quote is a fair character in a title; no existing client or expect file uses one (titles in the expect files: Sign in, Spy, Locked), but refusal moves the risk to every future client's error path. (C) strip them: silent loss, and a stripped title can become another's (`Sign in"` reads `Sign in`), an impersonation the escape avoids. Chosen: (A), re-implemented in displayd, not shared: displayd depends on libnawah and nawah-text only (user/apps/displayd/Cargo.toml), libui's put_quoted is private and writes libui's own 256-byte Text from decoded code points (user/libui/src/lib.rs:339, list.rs:119-127 pub(crate)); sharing would mean a public libui API or a move into nawah-text, both outside this package; both implementations are pinned by the same vectors (the quote, a newline, U+2028, U+202E, a long cut). Cut: the title gets 96 bytes in the line after naming; what does not fit is cut before the first unit (character or name) that does not fit, the line keeps its closing quote and event word and ends ` cut=<k>` (k units left out, at most 32); the mark goes at the end of the line, not right after the quote as in ui.md §3.9, so `" focused` and `" resized` stay adjacent for every reader; the line is at most 160 bytes, which the narrator's 256 holds even with every non-ASCII title byte written \u{…}. Storage: a title longer than TITLE_MAX is kept cut at a character boundary (drawing unchanged: draw_title already dropped the partial character, displayd main.rs:183-185). Failure modes: a title with the literal text [U+0022] or \u{0022} reads as a name (recorded limit, as ui.md §3.8/§3.9); invisible and quote-like characters pass as they are. Test: a new guest case TST-M5-WINDOW-TITLE (SVC-NT.TXT: the compositor and the narrator alone; no monitor step) with an exact transcript; SECURITY mutant M199 (the naming removed). The A11Y relay's attribution stays WP-103's.

found by the owner's external reviewer by reading commit fe456078 / 077628e1 and confirmed on 2026-11-15 by the team's independent verification (auditor by reading, security red team for who can trigger it; nothing run, no CI evidence): after one timeout the driver returns an error with the request still pending at the device (avail advanced, last_used not); the next request rewrites the same header, descriptors and buffer, and its wait ends on the late completion of the old one: wrong status and wrong data returned as Ok, a write's buffer refilled before the device read it, and last_used stays one behind for every later request until reboot; no reset path exists. Trigger: a slow or failing device or a stalled host, never a user process; no measurement of the timeout's duration exists; no test covers it

design to decide in the package (2-3 options with trade-offs): fail closed (a broken flag: every later request refused without touching the shared buffers) against a device reset and queue re-initialisation that restores service, against tracking the pending request with rotating heads; the first now, the second as a follow-up if chosen

test first, red seen locally before the fix: a test-kernel case with a ktest-only hook that makes one request time out (no notify, or a tiny poll limit), then reads a known sector: today the later request returns at once with an error or another request's data; expected: every later request is refused with the timeout's code (or correct data after a reset); a SECURITY mutant that drops the fail-closed check

Options: (A) fail closed: a stopped flag set in the timeout branch; read, write and flush refuse with K_E_BLK_NEEDS_RESET before they touch the shared buffer (write fills it before submitting, so the check sits there and not only in the request); (B) reset the device and re-initialise the queue: restores service, needs a bounded reset wait and a second init path; (C) track the pending request with rotating heads: more state, no answer for a dead device. Chosen: A now; B stays a possible follow-up. Test first, red seen locally: TST-M3-BLK-TIMEOUT in the test kernel with a ktest-only hook that withholds one request from the device and shortens its wait, so the driver's own timeout branch runs deterministically (publishing the request without a notify would depend on the emulator not polling the queue); a SECURITY mutant that drops the refusal

found by the owner's external reviewer by reading commit fe456078 / 077628e1 and confirmed on 2026-11-15 by the team's independent verification (auditor by reading, security red team for who can trigger it; nothing run, no CI evidence): delete and truncate free the cluster chain before the directory entry is rewritten: a failed entry write, a failed FSInfo write (advisory, yet it aborts the operation), a partial free or a power cut leaves a name that points at free clusters, which the next allocation hands to another file (cross-linked files, one file's data read through another's name); on a failed truncate the shared in-memory node keeps the freed chain for other open handles; a failed entry write after a data write leaves memory and disk different and sync does not write the entry again (a later successful write repairs it); a failed allocation leaks one cluster (safe order, bounded); the two FAT copies can differ after a failed second write (the kernel reads FAT0 only). Trigger: a device fault, a timeout (WP-104) or a power cut; the paths are reachable by any process on its own files, the failure is not. No test injects a write error

design to decide in the package (2-3 options with trade-offs): entry first, then free (the worst case becomes leaked clusters that fsck recovers) with or without a flush between them; FSInfo failure made non-fatal; the node zeroed before the free; a dirty mark on the node so that sync and close write the entry again; what the contract says about a failed write

test first, red seen locally before the fix: a ktest-only hook in block::write that fails the N-th write or a chosen sector, one case per failure point (entry write in unlink and in truncate, FSInfo write with two opens, entry write after a data write then close, reopen and stat), each followed by the host's tools/fat32.py check and fsck.fat -n on the image; SECURITY mutant: the order reversed

2026-11-15 sized before activation (a design brief by the kernel engineer, by reading; then the auditor, by reading and by experiments on a copy of tools/fat32.py in the scratch area, seen again by the manager; nothing run on the kernel, no CI evidence). Corrections to the lines above: (1) the host checks cannot judge a fault case as written: today's `fat32.py check` exits 0 on an image where a one-cluster file's first cluster is free in both FATs and on one where two files share a cluster, and `fsck.fat -n` exits 1 on every state the safe order itself leaves (a lost cluster, a stale FSInfo count, a chain longer than the size); so the package first strengthens `fat32.py check` (one seen-set over all files, a free first cluster, both FAT copies) and gives it a faulted mode that counts lost clusters, copy differences and longer chains and stays strict on an entry that points at a free cluster and on shared clusters; fsck.fat -n keeps running on the success-path cases with exit 0 required as today; (2) a failed write leaks up to the whole call's chain (at most 128 clusters: 64 KiB a call, one sector a cluster), not one cluster; (3) two states the finding did not name: store_entry failing in truncate after the whole chain was freed (the node is empty, the disk entry still points at the freed chain) and a chain longer than the size; (4) one N per operation does not show every failure point: the fault hook sweeps every write N of each operation, and a second boot reads the image again because the running kernel keeps its memory; (5) the hook imitates the disk after a cut following N-1 writes to the sector; it does not show writes reordered in a device cache, a torn sector or the unknown outcome of a timeout. Size: 130 to 160 calls by the engineer's estimate (unmeasured), over the budget line, so the package is split at a named point before activation: this package keeps the order of the three operations (delete: entry first, then free; truncate: a staged entry stored, then the node, then the free; write: the node after the stored entry), the fault hook and its sweep, the host checker and its host test, the mutants (one for each order) and the contract's text (files.md v1.5: the order and what a failed delete, truncate or write leaves; line 38 corrected to the shared node; ADR-0014 item 2); what depends on the disk's stop (the file system stopping with it, a flush between the two steps, FSInfo no longer fatal, the timeout case in two boots) is WP-117

2026-11-15 correction from the owner's reviewer (binding): fsck.fat is not dropped from the fault cases and its result is never hidden. Exit 0 alone cannot be the verdict where lost clusters are allowed, so in a fault case `fsck.fat -n` runs too, its whole output is kept in the evidence, and its messages are classified by the case: the set that may appear (lost clusters reclaimed, the free-cluster count, and whatever else the safe order is shown to leave) is named message by message before the fix, a message about shared clusters or about a file whose chain is shorter than its size fails the case, and a message the case does not name fails it as well. No acceptance condition is changed to get past it

Design chosen from the brief's options: delete = the entry first, then free_chain, answering the error of a failed free after the name is gone (a retry then answers not found; the contract says so); truncate = Err when the entry was stored and the free failed, the node equal to the disk; no flush between the steps here (WP-117). from WP-105's red team (2026-11-15, by reading, to check at activation): clusters lost by a failed delete or truncation are never given back and are not shown anywhere (free_clusters counts them as used; FSInfo's count stays stale because fsinfo_adjust works by difference; nothing is checked at mount); free_chain follows a chain that is already cross-linked into another file's clusters and frees them; free_chain stops silently at CHAIN_MAX

found by the security red team and by the auditor while reading WP-118 on 2026-11-15 (by reading; nothing run, no CI evidence; the manager read the same lines): any process can lose the volume's free space for good, with no device fault: a file with no first cluster (new, empty or truncated) is written, in one call, more than the free space holds (a call takes up to 128 clusters); the call takes what is free, answers no space and loses it; the process then deletes files of its own and does it again, up to 127 clusters a round; the loss outlives a reboot and only a repair tool outside the system gives it back. A call on a file that has a first cluster loses nothing on a full disk: its new clusters stay linked to its chain past the size

design to decide in the package (2-3 options with trade-offs): store what was written and answer the shorter count when the disk fills in the middle of a call (the bytes are on the disk and the count says so; the next call answers no space with nothing taken; callers must treat a short count as they treat it elsewhere) against freeing what the call took and answering no space with the file as it was (all or nothing; more writes on the failure path, each of which can fail) against asking for the free count before taking anything (a scan of the FAT for every call)

2026-11-21 (the manager): design. At most 16 launch attempts in a window of 1000 ticks for the whole manager (both requesters): the window starts at the first attempt after the last one ended; an attempt is a LAUNCH of a registered id that found a free place (the costly path: a job, a channel and an image read of up to 4 MiB), whatever its outcome (OK, ERR NOT_FOUND, ERR FAILED); the 17th and later in the window are answered ERR BUSY before any of it. ERR UNKNOWN and ERR FULL are cheap and not counted, nor is ERR BUSY itself, so a requester that retries never lengthens its own wait. Why 16 a second: TST-M6-APP-SPAWN's evidence of run 44849310736 took 7 s with its boot for 110 launches, about 20 ms each on CI, so 16 fit well inside a window and the case's refusal is not a matter of speed; a person does not start more than 8 applications a second and the table holds 8. Cost: TST-M6-APP-SPAWN's launcher retries ERR BUSY as it retries ERR FULL, about 7 s more of its 30. Case TST-M6-LAUNCH-RATE (new, M6, 30 s): the vouched session's lab role starts 16 that exit at once (ERR FULL retried, not counted), the 17th and 18th ERR BUSY, an unknown id ERR UNKNOWN in the full window, and after the window one more OK; services.md's next version states it. Inputs kept as limits: APPS from the desktop and a repeated READY (L-083), fairness between applications' channels (L-086), the lab role's reply buffer (L-081)
